Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, a warm welcome to the launch of the 2026 edition of the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World, known as SOFI Report. My name is Yasaman Matinroshan. I'm a Senior Technical Officer at FAO. Thank you. And I have the honor to moderate today's event. Before we begin, I would like to mention a few housekeeping notes. First of all, I would like to extend a warm welcome to everyone joining us online from around the world. I would like to mention that interpretation is available in all 6 official United Nations languages. And we also encourage you to join the conversation on social media using #SOFI2026. For a quarter of a century, the SOFI report has been published by FAO and UN partners. This year's report comes at a unique and critical moment. Intensifying climate extremes, Conflict, geopolitical tensions, and economic shocks are placing pressure on agri-food systems, threatening to deepen hunger and food insecurity while pushing healthy diet further beyond the reach of millions of people around the world. Over recent editions, SOFI has evolved beyond tracking hunger and food insecurity. SOFIE is assessing whether people can afford and consume healthy diets. To do this, it now combines the cost and affordability of a healthy diet with minimum dietary diversity indicators for children and women, including key nutrition outcomes: stunting, wasting, anemia, and obesity. Together, these measures show whether diets are affordable, diverse, and nutritionally adequate. This year's report goes beyond measuring these costs by examining the factors driving the costs and by identifying practical, evidence-based actions across agri-food systems to make healthy diets more affordable for all. As we move closer to 2030, today's discussion could not be more timely. And now, to set the stage for today's discussion, I draw your attention to our SOFI 2026 curtain-raiser video.

In a world marked by conflict, climate shocks, and economic uncertainty, it is easy to believe hunger can only get worse. But in 2025, world hunger fell for the 3rd consecutive year. An estimated 645 million people faced hunger, 14 million fewer than in 2024 and 43 million fewer than in 2022, according to the latest edition of the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report. The situation in Asia and Latin America and the Caribbean continues to improve. In Africa, the hunger rate declined for the first time in nearly a decade. The drop was small, and around 309 million Africans still faced hunger in 2025. And official development assistance to sub-Saharan Africa fell by 26.3%. Global health and nutrition indicators, meanwhile, show uneven progress. Just 31% of children under 2 and only 63% of all women achieve minimum dietary diversity. Adult obesity continues to rise. Child stunting, wasting, low birth weight, and exclusive breastfeeding are improving, but only marginally. Learning from countries making significant progress, we know that negative trends can be reversed, that the right mix of policies can make a difference. Countries are achieving results by combining investments in agriculture, social protection, health and nutrition, stronger markets, and rural infrastructure. When policies work together, hunger and malnutrition fall. Yet the recent gains are fragile and must be protected. Disruptions in critical trade corridors are raising energy, fertilizer, and transport costs, threatening future harvests. El Niño is strengthening, increasing the risk of damaging weather extremes. And preventing hunger is only one part of the challenge. About 2.69 billion people still cannot afford a healthy diet. Calories are relatively cheap. Healthy diets are expensive. Many of the costs accumulate after food leaves the farm as it is stored, processed, transported, and sold. Improving the efficiency of agri-food systems, especially for perishable, nutrient-dense foods that are central to healthy diets, can help lower those costs. The answer is not simply to spend more, More, it is to spend smarter. Progress is possible. Better and more affordable healthy diets for all are within our reach.

Thank you.

The increase is 25%, and this is because of commodity prices and, as a result of that, food inflation. But before we go into the details of the cost and the solutions to the problem of the cost, it's essential to define the precise scope of this year's report and set clear expectations about what it covers. To guide our analysis, the SOFI 2026 report is structured around the 4 critical pillars: understanding the numbers behind the food prices, determining the structural drivers that inflate those prices, and identifying the targeted interventions to bring them down, and finally, design the reforms needed to implement those changes. As the Director-General was saying, we need to implement and not to talk so much, so we need to start bringing solutions based on what we have learned so that countries can move forward. And that's— we have learned a lot, and that's what also the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty is bringing up through the pillar of knowledge. To ensure our policy focus remains sharp, we must be clear about what this report does not cover. First, our analysis is strictly focused on the economic conditions of healthy diets. Second, our primary lens is the absolute cost of a healthy diet. Finally, our framework is dedicated entirely to the solutions to reduce these costs across the agrifood value chains, rather than retaining the well-documented health or economic benefits of consuming a healthy diet. In short, this report provides a targeted supply-side blueprint where FAO has a huge— with our partners— a huge capacity to do. We are deconstructing the $4.28 PPP per capita to understand exactly why it remains so high and providing a roadmap to systematically dismantle the economic barriers keeping healthy diets out of reach to 2.7 billion people. It is vital to understand what this $4.28 figure actually measures. The cost of a healthy diet represents the absolute minimum market floor. It calculates the cheapest possible combination of locally available products across 6 strict food groups needed to meet dietary guidelines for 2,330 kilocalories. What this metric purposefully excludes are the hidden variables of real life. It ignores the heavy overhead cost of time, water, cooking fuel required for meal preparation, and it does not account for cultural preferences or convenience. Therefore, this $4.28 figure is a high conservative baseline. The true lived cost of putting healthy meals on the table is significantly higher for many families when we consider opportunity costs, which this report doesn't include right now. When we break down the composition— and this graph I think is very telling— of the average of healthy diets basket, we confront a fundamental imbalance in our agrifood systems: the calories versus the cost paradox. We see a massive disconnect between the dietary energy a food group provides and what it actually costs to the consumer. For example, starchy staples provide half of our daily required kilocalories— 50%— yet they only account, as you can see in the figure, to 60% of the cost of this healthy diet. In stark contrast, the highly nutritious foods we desperately need to combat malnutrition and to avoid overweight and obesity are disproportionately expensive. Fruits and vegetables, for example, together they provide just 13% of the required calories, but they represent a staggering 40% of the total diet cost. Similarly, animal-sourced foods supply another 30% of the calories but drive 28% of the financial burden. While these results are not surprising, they provide a key entry point to understand how and where to act. And again, understand that fruits and vegetables, animal foods require cooling chains, require better transportation, require food safety standards, and those are perishable goods and we need to find solutions to that so that the local costs can also decline. The global average of the $4.28 PPP dollars per capita per day masks also profound countries and regional disparities. At the global level, and to our surprise, it varies from 2 to 6. But the country differences are largely explained by regional differences, and the reality is that the price tag for a healthy diet is highly dependent on where you live. Surprisingly, Latin America and the Caribbean faces the highest average cost in the world, reaching $4.91 PPP dollars per person per day in 2025. As the charts indicate, this peak is heavily driven by the exorbitant retail price of highly perishable vegetables, direct results of severe domestic logistical friction and transport inefficiency. Amazing for a continent that is a bigger supplier of cereals and high-value commodities to the world. But this raises the question: we also need to look at our local markets. And yes, smallholder farmers, family farmers, are supplying the food for our local markets, but we need to work with them so that we increase the supply, especially for fruits and vegetables. In Africa, the cost stands at $4.35 PPP per person per day, but the primary culprit is completely different. Here, animal-sourced foods are the most prohibitively expensive food groups. This reflects deep structural challenges across the continent, including severe deficits in cold chains, high feed costs, and low baseline livestock productivity. And we also need to look at fisheries and aquaculture, how we can accelerate that, because this is the continent where more proteins are needed and enzymes, things that not only fish and aquaculture but also terrestrial animals bring. Meanwhile, Asia, where a diet costs $4.33 PPP, fresh fruits and vegetables heavily inflate the daily basket due to massive post-harvest losses. Conversely, North America, Europe and Oceania enjoy the lowest average cost, $3.64 PPP, as decades of capital-intensive policy support have made their staples and animal-sourced foods structurally cheap. The gradient between economic development and lower price is still statistically significant, but the relation is not simple. An increase in GDP by 10% translates into a reduction of healthy diets in 0.39%. Here is where growth doesn't resolve the problem. It has to be inclusive and we have to make the transformation to make it inclusive. So more efficient economies make healthy diets cheaper, but economic growth alone is not enough. How to fix this? And that's the goal of this report. The report identifies solutions along 2 complementary axes: expanding supply sustainably, reducing unit costs across the value chain, and to do this governments must bundle hardware and software interventions. Hardware refers to capital expenditures, investments in physical infrastructure like cold storage, rural roads and irrigation, as well as improved seeds. Software refers to regulatory reforms, repurposing agricultural subsidies, facilitating trade and enforcing competition policy. The critical lessons from our analysis is that we cannot run optimized software on broken hardware. Subsidy reforms— repurposing of subsidies— will fail to lower retail prices if severe infrastructure bottlenecks still exist, and we have learned a lot about it. Market incentives fail if physical capacity to store and move food does not exist. Both require simultaneous action. And now we have the capacity with our modeling tools and our data to assess those problems and to look at the whole value chains. We are talking a lot about corridors in Africa, but we need to overlay the corridors with productive potential, trying to see how we connect that infrastructure of roads, of irrigation, to agricultural potential. We cannot keep doing corridors around natural resources only, of mining or energy. We have to bring that to the potential of agriculture. That's what will make this possible and that's what will create the change. Moving to our next crucial finding, we must ask, where should we direct our investments to drive the largest price reductions? As this slide demonstrates, the right sectoral targeting of interventions matters enormously. So an impact of a 10% increase in efficiency at the global level on the hardware interventions, for example, in starchy foods, will reduce the cost to zero. More or less. In animal-sourced foods, in 2.3%, but in fruits and vegetables, in 9%, close to 1 to 1. So we know where to do this prioritization, we know where targeted interventions should happen so that we can reduce and have the target that we want to achieve. And we can look at this across regions. The right targeting of these hardware interventions matters and there is no universal blueprint. And here the intensity of the colours say what is the importance and you need to look at it by the columns because we are comparing across regions, not the horizontal one. For that we need more analysis and in the report you will see. But as you can see, there is diversity of what are the intensity of interventions across regions. In Latin America and the Caribbean, logistics, local logistics, domestic logistics are essential. Also, midstream distribution of markets and access to markets locally. But in other parts of the world, in Africa for example, post-harvest handling will be central, and also ensuring the cold chains so that we can move forward. So again, there is a huge diversity that we need to optimize and allocate our resources in the best possible way. To operationalize this transition, we propose 3 pillars of action. Pillar 1: target the midstream. We must relentlessly attack the 70-75% of food costs that accumulate post-farmgate through targeted hardware investments that eliminate physical food losses. Pillar 2: Update the software. We must halt the historical over-subsidization of starchy staples and redirect finite public research and development and fiscal transfers towards high-cost, highly perishable, nutrient-dense foods like fruits and vegetables. This needs to change. We have been repeating this for years. Pillar 3: we need to sequence for stability. We have learned a lot from the past. We learned from the quinoa example. We learned from other superfoods. We need to sequence interventions so that when we have foods that become extremely relevant for the world, the supply is ready. When they become extremely relevant for our local market, the supply is ready. We cannot just have and propose and incentivize a demand when we are not prepared for our supply. And that is where data, accountability, policy coherence, and public-private partnerships will help to move this trajectory. We need to accelerate this process because we are facing challenges. And let me finalize with looking ahead. What is ahead to us and what we can do by 2030 is extremely important. But there are many challenges that are ahead of us, and we are living some of them today. We have a huge geopolitical fracture. We have fiscal contraction in many of the countries which are facing significant challenge even to access the minimum calories they need. And we have weather extremes. We have violated 7 of the 9 planetary boundaries. We know for sure frequency and intensity of climate events will happen. So we need to be prepared for this. We need to be prepared for a world where value chains are no longer just-in-time but are just-in-case. We need to be prepared for a world where trade will be fragmented, to a world where the costs and inputs for agriculture are going to increase, and to a world where climate issues like El Niño, for example, could affect us even more and the compound effects could affect us even more. So we did some simulations on the trajectory and we see that, for example, just taking into account the Strait of Hormuz problem, we could be in a situation where we will be facing 522 million people by 2030 in hunger. And that's what we need to avoid. Now, we have 2 types of shocks: man-made and natural shocks. The man-made, I call them uncertainties. We don't have too much of a control, although we should have control because they are man-made. But the natural ones, we can increase our resilience, preventing and having capacity of absorption. And that's where we need to work to create this bridge where true food security requires systemic shifts to make nutrient-dense foods accessible to all, where we know for sure that we need to sustain calories available to protect the improvement of the 7.8% of our POU, but also we need to scale healthy diets affordability and target interventions to lower these costs of the healthy diet, which is at $4.28 PPP. So, colleagues, let me finish here with a summary of everything I have been talking for the last 24 minutes. And thank you so much, and let's hope that we can keep on track on what we are trying to do and we can really convert the change, and congratulating all the countries that have progressed so much in the last year. Thank you very much.
